Regular movement increases blood flow and brings oxygen and nutrients to joint cartilage, which can help joints work better and potentially last longer, thereby easing pain, stiffness, and fatigue while improving sleep and energy [1]. Aerobic, strengthening, and range-of-motion (ROM) exercises are the core at-home categories recommended for hip OA management, [1, 2]. - Aerobic exercise: Low-impact options like walking, biking, swimming, cross-country skiing, and elliptical training reduce joint stress while aiding weight control, which lowers load on the hip and can decrease pain; beginners should start with about 10 minutes and build up gradually toward a goal of 30 minutes, five days per week to minimize discomfort and injury [1]. - Strengthening: Stronger muscles better support and stabilize the hip, which can ease pain, slow further deterioration, and make daily tasks easier; options include resistance bands, light weights, tai chi, and yoga (which may also improve balance), and simple at-home moves such as repeated sit-to-stands, wall-supported partial squats, and single-leg stands for time, [1, 2]. - Range-of-motion and flexibility: ROM work helps ease stiffness and restore flexibility so you move more easily; examples include supported hip lunges with the torso upright and knee behind toes, knee-to-chest stretches on your back, and seated knee extensions, performed for multiple repetitions and held briefly to improve mobility; starting a few times per week and progressing to daily is suggested [2]. Low-impact activities are emphasized at the outset for people who haven’t been exercising, because they place less stress on the joints and lower the risk of flare-ups and injury as capacity builds [1]. Aquatic exercise (e.g., swimming or water aerobics) can be especially helpful by unloading the joint while allowing conditioning, and core strengthening can support the pelvis and lower back to offload the hip during weight-bearing activities, contributing to better mechanics and reduced stress at the hip,, [3, 4, 6]. As fitness improves, some individuals with mild-to-moderate OA may tolerate adding impact gradually, though this should follow a period of strength and endurance building to safeguard against injury, and those with severe OA should consult their physicians before attempting higher-impact or pivoting sports [2]. Practical progression and safety tips include beginning with short sessions, increasing duration incrementally over several days, and using support (a wall or chair) for balance as needed during ROM or balance drills to maintain good form and avoid strain, [1, 2]. Checking with your doctor before starting and choosing arthritis-appropriate classes or guided routines can further ensure that exercises are matched to your condition and goals [1]. If pain spikes or persists, adjust intensity, reduce impact, or seek professional guidance to modify the program appropriately, [1, 2].
